title: Hangul Monolith — Jamo Construction Poster
description: A single Hangul word towers at monumental scale, rendered in a modern geometric typeface with exposed jamo construction lines that double as structural diagram. Unlike decorative Korean templates, this one treats the letterform's internal geometry as the entire visual argument.
philosophy: This template exists because Hangul is already a designed object — each syllable block a grid-resolved architecture that most slides bury under decoration. It refuses multi-element layouts, color noise, and illustrative ornament, insisting that one word at extreme scale, with its skeletal construction lines visible, is more than enough to command a room. It is made for designers, cultural institutions, and speakers who understand that restraint is its own assertion. The tiny metadata block in the corner is not an afterthought but a deliberate echo of Ahn Sang-soo poster typography, where colophon and canvas coexist without hierarchy collapse.
goodFor: Typography and design conference keynote openers
Single-concept brand identity reveals for Korean-market campaigns
Cultural institution lecture title cards where the word is the entire argument
Film festival or documentary presentation title slides
avoidFor: Multi-bullet executive summary or status-update slides
Chart-heavy quarterly financial or data review decks
English-only audiences unfamiliar with Hangul jamo structure
Dense academic slides requiring footnotes, citations, or body paragraphs
author: harness

examples.promptCore: Monumental restraint: one Hangul word scaled to near-bleed becomes the slide's sole argument, carrying the weight of an architectural elevation drawing. Construction lines trace the jamo skeleton like a structural blueprint, turning calligraphic geometry into diagram rather than decoration. The surrounding void is active — it pressurizes the letterform the way negative space operates in editorial poster design, amplifying mass through silence. Avoid gradients, drop shadows, illustrative ornament, or any element that competes with the word's structural authority.

examples.layoutNotes: The Hangul word occupies near-full slide height, anchored optically at canvas center with a slight upward bias to counteract gravitational sag at extreme scale. Jamo construction lines extend as hairline overlays directly from the letterform's internal geometry, functioning simultaneously as architectural diagram and visual texture across the face of the glyph. A compact colophon block — deck name, presenter, date — stacks in tight lines at the bottom-left corner, maintaining minimal footprint against the surrounding void. No header band, no rule bar, no secondary illustration; the grid IS the letterform.

examples.promptCore: The slide reads as a typographic anatomy plate — clinical and architectural, with the reverence of a type-design construction study rather than a presentation aid. The exposed jamo skeleton does double duty: it is simultaneously the word's internal geometry and the slide's only diagram, so any secondary content feels like a schematic annotation rather than a bullet point. Compositional tension comes from the monolith's asymmetric placement against a disciplined open field, where silence carries as much weight as the letterform. Avoid decorative fill, illustrative ornament, gradient atmosphere, and any element that competes with the letterform's own structural argument.

examples.layoutNotes: The canvas runs edge-to-edge with no header band; a single Hangul word dominates the vertical axis, placed asymmetrically to carve expressive negative space on one flanking side. Jamo construction lines radiate from the letterform into the margins, functioning as both structural scaffold and content carrier — short annotations or a single-line concept phrase anchor directly to grid intersection points rather than sitting in a freestanding text block. A colophon-style metadata unit (section label, slide identifier) occupies the bottom corner at minimal scale, mirroring the title slide's poster logic. Hierarchy is achieved entirely through scale contrast; no ruled header strip, no dividing lines unrelated to the jamo geometry.
